scenes.visual: Dark slate background. Title 'Making Pulses and Fixing Place' centred in crisp white (size 48). Reuses the first film's exact colour map (amber = signal, teal = decoder/effector, bright green = active/kinase-favoured state, coral = inhibitor/phosphatase brake). A clean cross-section of a single cell begins drawing on the left with a live trace panel on the right.

scenes.tts: In the first film, a cell read how long a signal lasted and how fast spikes arrived. When an outside stimulus stays steady, how does a cell make pulses, or keep one signal local? Both answers come from how cells wire loops and organize space.
scenes.caption: In the first film, a cell read how long a signal lasted and how fast spikes arrived. When an outside stimulus stays steady, how does a cell make pulses, or keep one signal local? Both answers come from how cells wire loops and organize space.
scenes.visual: Carried world: a large cell cross-section (plasma membrane arc at top, cytoplasm in middle, nucleus oval at bottom) filling the left 60% of the frame, paired with a live trace panel on the right 35% (labelled 'schematic'). A flat steady amber beam hits the top membrane. On the right trace, a pulsing teal wave and a glowing local dot appear with a crisp white question mark between them.
scenes.narration: In the first film, a cell read how long a signal lasted and how fast spikes arrived. When an outside stimulus stays steady, how does a cell make pulses, or keep one signal local? Both answers come from how cells wire loops and organize space.

scenes.tts: Negative feedback normally pulls an active pathway back to a steady level. Add a delay, and the brake arrives late. Like a shower tap on a long pipe, you overshoot too hot, then too cold. When the feedback is strong and its proteins short-lived, activity can rise and fall in pulses.
scenes.caption: Negative feedback normally pulls an active pathway back to a steady level. Add a delay, and the brake arrives late. Like a shower tap on a long pipe, you overshoot too hot, then too cold. When the feedback is strong and its proteins short-lived, activity can rise and fall in pulses.
scenes.visual: Right trace panel compares two curves labelled 'schematic': a dashed grey curve ('No delay') settles flat immediately, while a solid teal curve ('With delay') overshoots up and down in smooth repeating pulses. Inside the cell on the left, a circular coral brake arrow with a small clock icon ('Delay') pulses in rhythm with the wave.
scenes.narration: Negative feedback normally pulls an active pathway back to a steady level. Add a delay, and the brake arrives late. Like a shower tap on a long pipe, you overshoot too hot, then too cold. When the feedback is strong and its proteins short-lived, activity can rise and fall in pulses.

scenes.tts: Watch N F kappa B inside this cell. A steady signal triggers destruction of its inhibitor, I kappa B, freeing N F kappa B to enter the nucleus. There, activation builds its own brake. N F kappa B switches on the gene for a fresh inhibitor, I kappa B alpha, which takes time.
scenes.caption: Watch NF-κB inside this cell. A steady signal triggers destruction of its inhibitor, IκB, freeing NF-κB to enter the nucleus. There, activation builds its own brake. NF-κB switches on the gene for a fresh inhibitor, IκBα, which takes time.
scenes.visual: Carried cell cross-section on the left, live nuclear NF-κB trace on the right (labelled 'schematic'). Steady amber stimulus at the top membrane breaks apart coral 'IκB' blocks holding teal 'NF-κB' in the cytoplasm. Free teal NF-κB glides into the nucleus; the right trace climbs into a bright-green peak. Inside the nucleus, NF-κB lights up 'IκBα gene', and a ticking delay bar fills slowly as new coral IκBα appears.
scenes.narration: Watch NF-κB inside this cell. A steady signal triggers destruction of its inhibitor, IκB, freeing NF-κB to enter the nucleus. There, activation builds its own brake. NF-κB switches on the gene for a fresh inhibitor, IκBα, which takes time.

scenes.tts: When fresh I kappa B alpha arrives, it binds N F kappa B and pulls it back out. Because the steady stimulus stays on, the new inhibitor breaks down too, starting the next pulse. Now stay in this cell to see place.
scenes.caption: When fresh IκBα arrives, it binds NF-κB and pulls it back out. Because the steady stimulus stays on, the new inhibitor breaks down too, starting the next pulse. Now stay in this cell to see place.
scenes.visual: New coral IκBα enters the nucleus, binds teal NF-κB, and carries it back to the cytoplasm; the right trace drops. The steady amber stimulus immediately breaks apart the coral IκBα again, and teal NF-κB streams back in, drawing a second and third pulse. Then the trace panel recedes as the camera glides smoothly up toward the cell's plasma membrane.
scenes.narration: When fresh IκBα arrives, it binds NF-κB and pulls it back out. Because the steady stimulus stays on, the new inhibitor breaks down too, starting the next pulse. Now stay in this cell to see place.

scenes.tts: One messenger can carry different orders in different spots of a cell. An anchoring protein parks the kinase P K A beside one membrane channel. A local cloud of cyclic A M P switches on that nearby P K A. Identical P K A parked across the cell may never see it.
scenes.caption: One messenger can carry different orders in different spots of a cell. An anchoring protein parks the kinase PKA beside one membrane channel. A local cloud of cAMP switches on that nearby PKA. Identical PKA parked across the cell may never see it.
scenes.visual: Top plasma membrane of the same cell cross-section fills the frame (labelled 'schematic'). Left side: a dark grey anchor ('AKAP') tethers teal 'PKA' right next to a channel. Right side: a second identical teal 'PKA' sits far away beside a different target. A localized amber cloud of 'cAMP' blooms on the left only, lighting the left PKA and its channel bright green while the distant right PKA stays dim teal.
scenes.narration: One messenger can carry different orders in different spots of a cell. An anchoring protein parks the kinase PKA beside one membrane channel. A local cloud of cAMP switches on that nearby PKA. Identical PKA parked across the cell may never see it.

scenes.tts: Proteins can also build a signaling spot on demand. On a glass slide with no cell, a kinase put phosphate on a receptor tail. Phosphates then reached the purified adaptor L A T. Many weak contacts pulled it and its partners into a liquid-like cluster that sorts enzymes.
scenes.caption: Proteins can also build a signaling spot on demand. On a glass slide with no cell, a kinase put phosphate on a receptor tail. Phosphates then reached the purified adaptor LAT. Many weak contacts pulled it and its partners into a liquid-like cluster that sorts enzymes.
scenes.visual: A crisp inset frame opens over the membrane, prominently badged 'Glass slide: purified proteins, no cell' (labelled 'schematic'). On a flat artificial lipid bilayer, amber phosphate tags appear on a receptor tail, then on teal LAT. Teal 'LAT' adaptors and partners drift together via dashed weak-contact lines and coalesce into a rounded translucent cluster.
scenes.narration: Proteins can also build a signaling spot on demand. On a glass slide with no cell, a kinase put phosphate on a receptor tail. Phosphates then reached the purified adaptor LAT. Many weak contacts pulled it and its partners into a liquid-like cluster that sorts enzymes.

scenes.tts: On the slide, that cluster pulls kinases in and keeps phosphatases, the enzymes removing phosphates, outside. Predict what happens inside the cluster. Compared with outside, will phosphate signals inside stay on longer, or shut off faster?
scenes.caption: On the slide, that cluster pulls kinases in and keeps phosphatases, the enzymes removing phosphates, outside. Predict what happens inside the cluster. Compared with outside, will phosphate signals inside stay on longer, or shut off faster?
scenes.visual: Inside the glass-slide cluster, bright-green 'Kinase' blocks crowd inward while coral 'Phosphatase' blocks bounce off the boundary and stay outside. Bold white question banner at top: 'Kinases in, phosphatases out: signals stay on longer, or shut off faster?' Two indicator bars shimmer gently: bright green rising ('Longer') vs coral dropping ('Faster').
scenes.narration: On the slide, that cluster pulls kinases in and keeps phosphatases, the enzymes removing phosphates, outside. Predict what happens inside the cluster. Compared with outside, will phosphate signals inside stay on longer, or shut off faster?

scenes.visual: Hold the glass-slide cluster with bright-green kinases drifting gently inside, coral phosphatases bouncing outside, and the question banner at top. A subtle white countdown ring ticks smoothly for 4.5 seconds.

scenes.tts: They stay on longer, because adding phosphates speeds up while removing them slows down. In living cells, the usual test bleaches a bright spot with a laser and times its refill. Refilling shows molecules exchange, which happens in a droplet and also on a fixed scaffold. So cellular droplets remain debated.
scenes.caption: They stay on longer, because adding phosphates speeds up while removing them slows down. In living cells, the usual test bleaches a bright spot with a laser and times its refill. Refilling shows molecules exchange, which happens in a droplet and also on a fixed scaffold. So cellular droplets remain debated.
scenes.visual: The cluster interior glows steadily bright green ('Signals stay on longer'). Then the inset closes back to the living cell cross-section, showing a glowing membrane spot with a split zoom box: left side 'Liquid droplet?' and right side 'Fixed scaffold?'. A brief white laser beam dims the spot and the spot refills as teal molecules swap in equally in both halves; badge reads 'Living cells: still debated'.
scenes.narration: They stay on longer, because adding phosphates speeds up while removing them slows down. In living cells, the usual test bleaches a bright spot with a laser and times its refill. Refilling shows molecules exchange, which happens in a droplet and also on a fixed scaffold. So cellular droplets remain debated.

scenes.tts: Cells encode meaning in feedback loops and in space, not just in molecule names. Delayed negative feedback turns steady cues into pulses, and location decides which targets answer. Read on for circuits that test both.
